en: The Apadāna of the Elder Yāgudāyaka Bhaddāli-vagga 8 I was once a poor man, a beggar, living in the city of Benares. At that time, the Buddha, the Teacher, was dwelling in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Having heard of the arrival of the Buddha, the Great Sage, the One with Vision, I went to him, and having approached, I offered him a bowl of rice gruel. Because of that gift of rice gruel, I was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-three gods. There, for eighty-four thousand aeons, I enjoyed celestial bliss. When my lifespan there had expired, I was reborn in the human world. In every birth, I was wealthy, prosperous, and possessed of great merit. For eighty-four thousand aeons, I never experienced suffering. I was always handsome, fortunate, and endowed with great splendor. I was born into noble families, and I always lived in comfort. Through the power of that root of merit, I have now attained the state of an Arhat. Having seen the Truths, I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra. I have paid homage to the Buddha, the Teacher, the One with Vision. By this truth, may there be well-being for all beings everywhere. May all dangers be dispelled; may all misfortunes cease. May all beings be happy; may they be free from all suffering. Thus did the Elder Yāgudāyaka speak his own ancient history.
“Having taken my guest,
I then went to the village;
seeing a river that was full to the brim, I thought:”
I approached the monastery.
There were forest-dwellers, upholders of the ascetic practices,
meditators wearing coarse robes;
Delighting in discernment, those wise ones dwell in the monastery of the Sangha;
their course of rebirth has been cut off.
Those who are well-liberated and poised do not go for alms,
for they are like rivers that have been dammed.
With a clear mind and a joyful heart,
filled with rapture and with palms joined in reverence,
having taken rice from me—
I gave a gift of rice gruel.
Having given rice gruel to five [monks],
with my own hands and full of faith;
Delighted by my own deeds,
I went to the realm of the Thirty-three;
there my celestial mansion was made of jewels.
I was reborn among the hosts of the Thirty-three;
accompanied by throngs of women,
I rejoice in this most excellent celestial mansion.
Thirty-three times I exercised sovereignty as Lord of the Gods,
and thirty times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
I exercised great sovereignty;
my regional kingdoms were vast,
beyond all calculation.
Having personally experienced [the fruits] in the world of the gods or among humans,
when my final existence has arrived—
I went forth into homelessness;
as soon as my hair was shorn,
I fully penetrated everything.

Contemplating the body as it decays and disintegrates, even before the undertaking of the training rules, one reflects thus: "This body will surely become like this. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the charnel ground, sees a corpse discarded in the cemetery—one day, two days, or three days dead—bloated, livid, and festering, he compares his own body with that: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of the same character, and not exempt from that fate. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the charnel ground, sees a corpse discarded in the cemetery, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various kinds of small creatures, he compares his own body with that: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of the same character, and not exempt from that fate. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the charnel ground, sees a corpse discarded in the cemetery, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews... a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood, held together by sinews... a skeleton without flesh or blood, held together by sinews... disconnected bones scattered in all directions: here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, here a hip-bone, there a spine, here a skull... bones bleached to the color of shells... bones heaped up... bones more than a year old, rotted and crumbled to dust, he compares his own body with that: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of the same character, and not exempt from that fate. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, enclosed by the skin and full of many kinds of impurities: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine"—he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, by way of its elements: "In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element"—he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: "I breathe in long"; or breathing out long, he knows: "I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he knows: "I breathe in short"; or breathing out short, he knows: "I breathe out short. He trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, knows: "I make a long turn," or when making a short turn, knows: "I make a short turn," so too, a bhikkhu, when breathing in long, knows: "I breathe in long"; or breathing out long, he knows: "I breathe out long" ... [as above] ... he trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. Or else, he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the body both its nature of arising and its nature of passing away. "Mindfulness of breathing, indeed, is established in him to the extent necessary for mere knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements: "In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element"—he dwells contemplating the body in the body. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he contemplates the body as a body. He perceives the body as impermanent, not as permanent; he perceives the body as suffering, not as happiness; he perceives the body as non-self, not as self; he perceives the body as repulsive, not as attractive. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. Or else, he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the body both its nature of arising and its nature of passing away. "Mindfulness of the body, indeed, is established in him to the extent necessary for mere knowledge and mindfulness.

And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. This is called the contemplation of the body in the body. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he contemplates feelings as feelings. When feeling a pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel a pleasant feeling"; when feeling a painful feeling, he knows: "I feel a painful feeling"; when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. When feeling a worldly pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel a worldly pleasant feeling"; when feeling an unworldly pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel an unworldly pleasant feeling"; when feeling a worldly painful feeling, he knows: "I feel a worldly painful feeling"; when feeling an unworldly painful feeling, he knows: "I feel an unworldly painful feeling"; when feeling a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"; when feeling an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows: "I feel an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally. Or else, he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in feelings both their nature of arising and their nature of passing away. "Mindfulness of feelings, indeed, is established in him to the extent necessary for mere knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. This is called the contemplation of feelings in feelings. Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he contemplates mind as mind. He knows a mind with lust as a mind with lust; he knows a mind without lust as a mind without lust. He knows a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; he knows a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred. He knows a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; he knows a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion. He knows a contracted mind as a contracted mind; he knows a distracted mind as a distracted mind. He knows a great mind as a great mind; he knows an immeasurable mind as an immeasurable mind. He knows a surpassed mind as a surpassed mind; he knows an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind. He knows a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; he knows an unconcentrated mind
I attained the state of an arahant.
My excellent gift was well-bestowed,
and my trade was successfully engaged.
By that very gift of rice gruel,
I have attained the unshakable state,
free from sorrow, lamentation, and disease.
I do not recall ever experiencing distress or mental anguish that has arisen;
this is the fruit of giving rice gruel.
Having given rice-gruel to the Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit,
I experience five benefits.
Oh, how delightful is the offering of gruel!
To be free from illness, to be endowed with beauty,
and to quickly settle into the Dhamma— these are the fruits thereof.
The obtaining of food and drink,
and life as the fifth— these are mine.
Whoever produces this [knowledge], [attains them].
One should give rice-gruel to the Saṅgha;
a wise person should accept these five things.
All that was to be done has been done;
existence has been shattered by me;
all taints are utterly exhausted.
Now there is no further becoming.
Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town.
Paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the excellent nature of the Dhamma,
for thirty thousand eons—
The gift that I gave back then—
I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of that offering of rice gruel.
The defilements have been burnt away by me; ... [as before] ...
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me...
[and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges...
[and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed the venerable elder Yāgudāyaka spoke these verses.
This is the eighth legend of the elder Yāgudāyaka.
